candidate.draft:
Grinding hip stretches and still stuck above parallel? Your ankles—not your hips—decide how deep you can squat.

We’re the crew chasing clean depth, so we’re using an ankle-first lens—dorsiflexion sets knee travel, torso angle, and bottom room more than hip work does. See your squat through your ankles and the warm-ups and cues start making sense.

Your dorsiflexion sets how far your knees can travel; when it’s limited, your hips shift back and your torso tips forward, capping depth even if the hips feel “mobile” (per Macrum 2012). In controlled squats, restricting ankle motion cut knee flexion and increased trunk lean, while adding a heel lift allowed deeper, more upright squats by lowering dorsiflexion demand (per Macrum 2012; Sato 2012). Screen it with a weight‑bearing lunge and, if stiff, spend warm-ups on calf/soleus eccentrics, tibialis raises, and heel-elevated patterning instead of endless hip openers. See the squat through your ankles and your depth will follow.

Squatting on tight ankles is like steering a shopping cart with a locked front wheel—when the front end won’t roll forward, you’re forced to swing your hips back and lean just to keep going, but a little heel lift frees the “wheel” so you drop deeper and more upright.

Comment ANKLE for the 1-minute dorsiflexion warm-up and weight-bearing lunge test follow-up.
